title: Elijah, come soon
hook: after Havdalah, a song for Elijah, who is to announce redemption

segments.voice: Yesterday, the verses of trust that open Havdalah. Your line was I will trust. Did you say it before something hard? Today, the song that comes right after the candle goes out. Day six hundred twenty-five.

The Havdalah candle is dipped into the spilled wine, and it goes out with a hiss. The room is darker now. Shabbat is over. And then, almost every time, people start singing about a man who never died. Eliyahu hanavi. Elijah the prophet. It's the same Elijah we met on Mount Carmel, calling down fire in the afternoon. But here he's not a figure from a story. He's someone the song asks to show up, soon, maybe this very week.
screen: `THE CANDLE HISSES OUT.` → `A SONG ABOUT A MAN WHO NEVER DIED.` → `MAYBE THIS VERY WEEK.`

segments.voice: First, why never died? In the book of Kings, Elijah doesn't die the way others do. He's walking with his student Elisha, and a chariot of fire and horses of fire come between them, and Elijah goes up by a whirlwind into heaven. The text never records his death. So in Jewish tradition, he's still around. Then the promise. The very last words of the prophets in the Hebrew Bible, in Malachi, say, in the old Jewish translation: "Behold, I will send you Elijah the prophet before the coming of the great and terrible day of the LORD." And he will turn the hearts of parents to children, and the hearts of children to their parents. So Elijah becomes the one who announces redemption, the herald who comes before the messiah. The song is simple. Elijah the prophet, Elijah the Tishbite, Elijah the Gileadite. May he come to us soon, in our days, with the messiah, son of David. Why sing it on Saturday night? There's a tradition, drawn from the Talmud, that Elijah won't arrive on Shabbat itself, so as not to disturb it. Once Shabbat ends, the door is open again. So the song is a kind of hope at the start of the week: maybe this week. Elijah shows up all over Jewish life. A cup is filled for him at the Passover seder, and the door is opened. A chair is set for him at a baby boy's circumcision. In folk stories he appears in disguise, a beggar, a stranger, to help someone in trouble.
screen: `UP BY A WHIRLWIND.` · `I WILL SEND YOU ELIJAH.` · `NOT ON SHABBAT, SO NOW.` · `A CUP, A CHAIR, A STRANGER.` · then, large: `ELIJAH, COME SOON.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: hope for the week ahead. Settle, and breathe. Malachi says Elijah will turn the hearts of parents and children toward each other. Think of one relationship in your life where a heart could turn. Picture this week bringing one small turn: a call returned, a kind word, a door opened. Don't plan it. Just hope it. Hold that hope gently, like a cup waiting to be filled. The bell holds the time.
Eliyahu hanavi. Elijah the prophet. The one who went up in a whirlwind, sung for every Saturday night as the herald of redemption.
Your line: elijah, come soon. This week, be someone's unexpected helper, the stranger who turns up at the right moment. Day six hundred twenty-five.

howItsDone: Eliyahu HaNavi is sung at the end of Havdalah on Saturday night in many homes and synagogues; Elijah also has a cup at the Passover seder and a chair at a brit milah.

fork.setup: Shabbat has just ended, the candle is out. why sing for Elijah right now?
options: because he died on a Saturday.
because tradition says he won't come on Shabbat, so now he might.
fork.reveal: a tradition from the Talmud holds Elijah won't come on Shabbat; once it ends, maybe this week.

trapdoor: what you thought: a folk song about an old prophet.
what it means: a weekly hope that redemption could begin this week, sung as Shabbat ends.
what a scholar hears: 2 Kings 2:11's whirlwind, Malachi 3:23–24's promise, and Eruvin 43b's discussion of Elijah and Shabbat.

sources.quoted: Behold, I will send you Elijah the prophet before the coming of the great and terrible day of the LORD.

notes: Malachi 3:23 quoted from JPS 1917 from memory; verify (JPS numbering 3:23; KJV 4:5).

Eruvin 43b: Elijah will not come on Shabbat eve; the custom of singing for Elijah after Havdalah is explained this way in later sources (e.g., Tur OC 295); simplified to 'won't arrive on Shabbat itself'. Confirm.
Malachi as the last book of the Prophets in the Hebrew Bible (end of Nevi'im); confirm phrasing 'last words of the prophets'.
